posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
Akkari said:
People just don't like any form of Copy Protection and DRM stuff.
Click to expand...
So to clarify something here, Enigma Virtual Box is more like a form of tamper protection and not copy protection.
The distinction here is that it prevents modifying files easily, but it doesn't stop a user from copy-pasting the installation onto to a USB drive and taking it to another computer.
I have never heard of a single person complain about tamper protection. That's not to say they don't exist, I'm sure there are some crazy people out there who feel entitle to every file in a game's directory, however I think most people complain about digital rights management (DRM) which is more-often-than-not about copy protection and not tamper protection.
It's certainly reasonable for a dev to want tamper protection. Yes, at the end of the day anyone with enough time and motivation can crack any form of software protection, but at least some protection helps keep the honest folk honest and doesn't tempt them from doing something they shouldn't.
Tamper protection allows protection of assets, which prevents people from ripping them to use in their own game. This can include images, sound, and even code; in the case of MV/MZ games, copying a plugin could allow someone to basically steal wholly unique mechanics to a game, so it's not unreasonable to want at least some basic protection over that (though, actually no
adequate
form of plugin protection really exists)

posts.author: Artille
posts.body:
Cherry said:
Assets are one thing (and more difficult). But another thing, and what I was mainly talking about, was the desire to prevent people from looking at the structure and "logic" of the game. The question was about how to stop people from opening the game in the editor, not from looking into the resource folders. I still don't see the point here.
Click to expand...
Unless I'm missing something, you can't just open a published game in your editor—it simply doesn't work that way.
As for the original question, "How do I protect my assets?"
Simple answer:
You can't.
The reason is straightforward: the game is "downloaded" as an app, package, or whatever you call it, but once it's local, everything is accessible. Anything running locally must be readable by some kind of software, and with the right tools, anyone can extract everything at the right moment.
You can encrypt, minify, uglify, obfuscate as much as you want, but given enough time (and since it's local, there's no time limit), anyone with the right tools can break it down.
Code simply cannot be fully hidden.
Assets can be encrypted, and I like my idea of "puzzlefying" images, though even that isn't unhackable. Here's the concept:
Create a tool that processes all your images.
Break each image down into smaller pieces (8x8 pixels, or even smaller) and combine them into a binary file.
Encrypt this with a session key, so every game launch will require a new key to read it.
Write a plugin that calls a remote server for decryption, which sends the necessary data back to the client.
Add this into a loading feature to prevent lag when reconstructing the images.
This could also be applied to sound files, but it comes with the drawback of requiring an internet connection. If the player can't connect to the server, they can't play the game.
Ultimately, there's little you can do to prevent a determined hacker from getting everything. You can only make it harder, to the point where most will move on. Hackers are generally not interested in games that are difficult to hack unless there's significant financial motivation (like a very successful game).

You can. Simply use RPG Maker's "Open Project" dialog to open the game's folder. (Select the parent folder as base path so the game folder itself is listed as project within.) Alternatively, drag any of the files in the game's main directory, such as the EXE file, onto RPG2003.exe.
